fields.definition: A stored set of static mixer parameter values, such as fader levels, pans, sends, mutes, and plug-in settings, captured at one instant and recalled as an immediate step change rather than as time-varying moves.
fields.plain_english: A saved photo of all your mixer settings at one moment. You can load it later to snap every fader and knob back to those exact positions.
fields.purpose_function: It lets an engineer store and recall a whole console or mixer state so different scenes, sections, or songs can be reset instantly and repeatably.
fields.practical_application: A live engineer stores a snapshot for each song so the desk reconfigures at the touch of a button, and a studio engineer snapshots a starting balance before trying changes.
common_mistakes: Confusing a snapshot, which is an instant static jump, with dynamic automation that records moves over time
Forgetting that firing a snapshot overwrites current settings, causing an abrupt jump if triggered at the wrong moment
Not re-saving a snapshot after tweaking settings, so the recall restores old values
scenario_contexts: Recalling a full desk setup for each song in a live show
Storing a baseline mix balance before experimenting during a session
Resetting a console to a known state at the start of a rehearsal

sources: Sound on Sound, 'Introduction To Mixer Automation'

fields.definition: An automation mode that records relative offsets to existing automation rather than absolute values; nudging a control adds or subtracts that amount from the underlying automation curve while preserving its shape.
fields.plain_english: An automation mode that saves changes as a little louder or a little quieter instead of exact levels. It keeps the shape of your old moves and just shifts them up or down.
fields.purpose_function: It lets an engineer adjust an overall level or balance across a passage without erasing the detailed automation moves already written underneath.
fields.practical_application: After writing detailed vocal rides, an engineer switches to trim to raise the whole vocal by a decibel through the chorus while keeping every existing move intact.
common_mistakes: Thinking trim writes absolute levels when it only adds an offset to what is already there
Forgetting to coalesce or commit trim moves, leaving a separate trim layer that confuses later edits
Leaving a channel in trim when a fresh absolute pass was intended
scenario_contexts: Raising a whole vocal line a decibel while keeping existing rides
Balancing a submix level without redoing detailed automation
Making a global correction after a client asks for more guitar throughout

sources: Apple Logic Pro User Guide (automation modes)

fields.definition: The function that reverses the most recent automation edit or recorded pass, restoring the automation data to its previous state within the project's edit history.
fields.plain_english: A button that takes back your last automation change. If a move sounds wrong, undo puts the settings back the way they were.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the engineer a safety net to experiment with automation freely, since any unwanted move can be reversed step by step.
fields.practical_application: After a fader pass goes wrong, the engineer hits undo to drop the bad automation and try the ride again from the previous version.
common_mistakes: Assuming undo can recover automation from before the project was closed, when the history usually clears on close
Undoing past an intended point and losing good edits along with the bad one
Confusing undo of an automation pass with disabling automation playback
scenario_contexts: Reversing a botched fader ride during mixing
Stepping back through several automation edits to find a better take
Recovering the previous curve after an accidental overwrite

sources: Sound on Sound, 'Automation Facilities In Pro Tools'

fields.definition: How well a finished mix keeps its intended tonal balance, clarity, and level relationships when played over a car audio system, which is one of the most common real-world environments used to check whether a mix holds up.
fields.plain_english: How good your mix sounds when you play it in a car. Cars have odd speakers and road noise, so a mix that holds up there usually works almost anywhere.
fields.purpose_function: Checking a mix in a car reveals balance and low-end problems that a treated studio can hide, helping ensure the mix works on the systems most listeners actually use.
fields.practical_application: After finishing a rough mix, an engineer bounces it to a phone and listens in the car to judge whether the vocal, bass, and kick still sit right.
common_mistakes: Judging a car listen at very high volume, which flatters the low end and misleads decisions
Trusting only one car and treating its coloured sound as the truth
Making big EQ moves by ear in the car without confirming them back on studio monitors
scenario_contexts: Checking a near-final mix on the drive home from the studio
Comparing a mix to a commercial reference track in the same car
Spotting excess or weak bass that the studio room masked

sources: Bob Katz, Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science

flags: All fields left blank: 'B-side assignment' has no established, attested meaning in professional mix or workflow literature. 'B-side' is a music-business/vinyl term and 'assignment' is a routing term, but the combination is not a recognized audio-engineering concept and is not defined in any acceptable standards body, manufacturer technical doc, or professional text. Not a transparent technique-plus-source compound, so it is ambiguous rather than authorable.

fields.definition: In audio post-production, a consolidated intermediate mix of all the background (ambience/atmosphere) sound effects, balanced and processed as a group before the final re-recording mix so the many background tracks can be handled as one manageable element.
fields.plain_english: A rough mix that blends all the background sounds, like room tone, traffic, or wind, into one tidy group. It gets the atmospheres balanced early so the final mix has fewer things to juggle.
fields.purpose_function: It reduces a huge number of background tracks to a controllable sub-mix, letting the re-recording mixer set the overall ambience level quickly during the final mix.
fields.practical_application: A sound editor premixes dozens of city-ambience tracks into a backgrounds premix so the dub-stage mixer can ride one background level against dialogue and effects.
common_mistakes: Baking in too much level or EQ so the final mixer loses room to adjust the backgrounds
Confusing a backgrounds premix, which is a working sub-mix, with a delivered stem
Printing backgrounds too loud against dialogue, forcing rework at the dub stage
scenario_contexts: Consolidating many ambience tracks before a film's final dub
Preparing TV episode atmospheres so the mix stage runs efficiently
Balancing crowd and room tones as one element ahead of the final mix

sources: Tomlinson Holman, Sound for Film and Television
David Lewis Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: A delivered stem containing only the background (ambience/atmosphere) elements of a mix, isolated from dialogue, music, and foreground effects, so the backgrounds can be recalled, replaced, or re-balanced independently.
fields.plain_english: A separate audio file that holds just the background sounds of a scene, with no dialogue or music. It lets someone later change or reuse the atmospheres on their own.
fields.purpose_function: It exists so backgrounds can be adjusted, muted, or swapped later, for example during foreign-language versions or re-edits, without touching the other elements.
fields.practical_application: A studio delivers a backgrounds-only stem so a foreign-language dub can keep the original ambiences while replacing the dialogue.
common_mistakes: Leaving foreground spot effects or dialogue bleed in what should be a clean backgrounds stem
Confusing a backgrounds-only stem with a full effects stem that also holds hard effects
Not matching the stem's level and processing to the final mix, so it will not sum back correctly
scenario_contexts: Delivering separated stems for a film's international versions
Rebalancing ambience level during a client revision without a full remix
Reusing scene atmospheres in a trailer or re-edit

sources: Tomlinson Holman, Sound for Film and Television
David Lewis Yewdall, Practical Art of Motion Picture Sound

fields.definition: Unwanted sound from the stage backline, such as guitar and bass amps or the drum kit, that leaks into microphones intended for other sources, colouring those channels and reducing separation.
fields.plain_english: When loud gear on stage, like guitar amps or drums, bleeds into microphones meant for other things. The extra sound leaks in and makes each channel harder to control.
fields.purpose_function: It names a common cause of poor separation on stage, and recognizing it guides microphone choice, placement, and stage layout so channels stay cleaner.
fields.practical_application: Hearing a guitar amp in the vocal mic, an engineer angles or moves the amp, chooses a tighter cardioid mic, or gates the channel to cut backline spill.
common_mistakes: Trying to EQ out spill instead of fixing stage volume or mic placement, which rarely works
UNSAFE: Raising stage monitor and amp levels to mask spill, driving stage SPL to levels that risk hearing damage over a show
Gating too hard so wanted parts of the source get chopped along with the spill
scenario_contexts: A loud guitar amp bleeding into the lead vocal mic at a club gig
Drum spill into vocal mics blurring a live recording of the band
Bass amp energy leaking into every open channel on a small stage

sources: Sound on Sound, 'Working With Mic Bleed'

fields.definition: A transition, edit, or arrangement change placed exactly on a bar (measure) boundary so it lands in time with the musical grid, keeping the groove intact across the change.
fields.plain_english: A change in the music, like a new section or a cut, that lands right at the start of a bar. Because it hits on the beat grid, the switch feels smooth and in time.
fields.purpose_function: Aligning transitions to bars keeps edits musical and rhythmically seamless, which is essential for looping, arranging, and joining sections without breaking the pulse.
fields.practical_application: When rearranging a song in a DAW, an engineer snaps the cut between verse and chorus to the downbeat of a bar so the join sounds natural.
common_mistakes: Cutting on the visual waveform instead of the bar line, so the edit drifts off the beat
Ignoring pickup notes that start before the bar, which get chopped off by a strict bar cut
Assuming a bar-aligned cut is beat-perfect when the project tempo map is wrong
scenario_contexts: Snapping a verse-to-chorus cut to the downbeat while arranging in a DAW
Building a seamless loop that repeats cleanly every bar
Editing a live recording so section joins stay in time

sources: Sound on Sound (editing and arranging techniques)
